newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lawyers say German charges filed against tycoon.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers say German charges filed against tycoon.

text.p: Lawyers for Juergen Schneider, blamed for one of the most spectacular corporate collapses in German history, said on Sunday German prosecutors have filed criminal charges against the disgraced property tycoon.
Schneider's lawyer, Christoph Rueckel, did not detail the charges against Schneider but he has previously said they would include fraud, falsifying documents and fraudulent bankruptcy.

Frankfurt prosecutors will hold a news conference on Monday to announce details of the charges against Schneider, whose property empire collapsed in April 1994 under the weight of some five billion marks in debt.
A trial is not expected to start before mid-1997.

Rueckel said the 62-year-old Schneider, who was once one of Germany's most celebrated entrepreneurs, was committed to fighting the allegations and reiterated that German banks which lent money to Schneider were also responsible for his collapse.
"The quality of the allegations will be measured by whether the joint responsibility of the banks is reflected," Rueckel said in a statement.

The charges are expected to allege that Schneider received credit on the basis of falsified documents, such as overstating expected rental income. He then slid into bankruptcy as the rental income was too low to service the mounting debt.

Schneider's disappearance in April 1994 as his empire collapsed, and later the bankruptcy of his group, exposed his creditor banks to hefty public outrage at the apparent ease with which he obtained funding from them.
Deutsche Bank AG, the country's largest commercial bank and Schneider's biggest creditor, bore the brunt of public criticism over a perceived lack of supervision.

Deutsche chief executive Hilmar Kopper made matters worse by dismissing as "peanuts" the millions of marks Schneider owed to small tradesmen and builders, many of whom had to file for bankruptcy after not being paid for their services.
Schneider and his wife, Claudia, were detained in Miami in 1995 following a year-long international manhunt. They returned voluntarily to Germany last February to face questioning.
Claudia Schneider, who has been freed from prison on conditional release amid concerns about her health, is expected to be charged with being an accessory to bankruptcy.
Schneider, who ran his empire from a flamboyant castle-like villa in the Taunus Hills near Frankfurt, has been detained in a Frankfurt area prison since his return to Germany.
Two former associates, Mehdi Djawadi, alleged to have helped the Schneiders plan their getaway, and Karl-Heinrich Kuepferle are also expected to be charged.

Schneider, a bricklayer turned property magnate, specialised in buying and refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls, purchasing some of Germany's most prestigious real estate in the post-unification property boom.

One of his properties was a Leipzig building which housed Auerbach's Cellar, a drinking hall featured in Goethe's plan "Faust" in which a man sells his soul to the devil in return for wealth and power -- and ends up being dragged off to hell.
